a.xlink:title: C · Ordinary return and exceptional acquisition come from one verse, warranting their comparison.
R · The comparison places ordinary recoverable loss under the prohibition with or without a mark, within that prohibition’s temporal scope.
C · The verse does not state the permission alongside the prohibition; it excludes the inaccessible case from the prohibition. Ritva records this objection as coming from Tosafot.

a.xlink:title: R · Suppose the comparison transfers all awareness and despair conditions unchanged from exceptional permission to ordinary prohibition.
C · If every condition were transferred, ordinary loss would remain prohibited even after actual despair. Ritva records this objection as coming from Tosafot.
R · Ordinary loss would be prohibited even after actual despair. This is the consequence challenged by the reported objection, not Rashi’s qualified conclusion.
C · For ordinary loss, actual despair before pickup can permit acquisition, including a marked object whose owner knowingly despairs.
C · Read loss and finding together: the verse addresses a find immediately following the loss, before the owner knows.
C · In that unaware-at-finding case, the verse opens permission only for loss to everyone; the ordinary prohibition also covers unmarked loss.
C · Permission after the owner knows, for an unmarked loss, is derived separately from the garment passage (simlah).

a.xlink:title: C · On this reading, ordinary unmarked loss found before awareness is prohibited; established prior despair remains outside that temporal case.
